The paper proposes an automatic workflow for assessing damage on gas turbine blades using deep learning-based instance segmentation on borescope video feeds.
The workflow can track individual blades across frames and extract damage statistics for each blade, enabling a more comprehensive assessment compared to manual inspection.
The neural network architecture used is Mask R-CNN with a ResNet50-FPN backbone, and the PointRend module is incorporated to improve segmentation accuracy.
The algorithm for tracking blades across frames assumes a high frame rate relative to the blade rotation speed and that blades travel approximately horizontally.
Damage is quantified as a fraction of the projected area of the blade visible in each frame, allowing for a comprehensive assessment across the full blade trajectory.
A post-processing step involving high-pass filtering, masked erosion, and thresholding is introduced to improve the detection of small surface damage marks.
Out of 4,881 video frames, 104 images were manually labeled and used for training (89 images) and testing (15 images).
The training loss continued decreasing with more iterations, but the testing loss started increasing after around 200 iterations, indicating overfitting.
The detection quality improved when comparing the network at a later stage of training (2,000 iterations) to an earlier stage (500 iterations).
The mean average precision (mAP) and mean matched IoU are used as performance metrics for the instance segmentation network.
The mAP score increased significantly as the network was trained for more iterations, while the mean matched IoU remained relatively constant.
The paper aims to classify multiple types of damage, including surface damage, material separation, and material deformation, unlike previous work that focused on only a single type of damage.
The paper also aims to deduce the structure of the scene by separately identifying multiple blades, unlike previous work that only performed semantic segmentation.
The introduction of the post-processing step helps address the challenge of detecting small surface damage marks on the blades, which are difficult to identify through manual inspection.
The automatic workflow proposed in the paper can remove human biases, enable faster decision-making, and quantify uncertainty via confidence scores, compared to manual borescope inspections.
